newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks hail Berne's help on Holocaust funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks hail Berne's help on Holocaust funds.

text.p: Swiss banks on Monday welcomed the appointment of a Foreign Ministry troubleshooter to counter mounting allegations that Switzerland cynically profitted from bank deposits left by Jews killed in the Holocaust.

The Swiss Bankers Association said diplomat Thomas Borer, head of a new task force on the fate of assets of Nazi victims, would help speed existing efforts to answer a barrage of allegations by Jewish groups and an influential U.S. senator.
"I expect this will increase cooperation (between the government and banks) and thereby enhance transparency and efforts to resolve open questions," association spokesman Silvia Matile said.

Borer on Friday was put in charge of formulating Berne's response to sharp criticism from the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and Senator Alfonse D'Amato that Swiss politicians and bankers say is damaging the neutral country's reputation.
Borer, known in Berne as a favourite troubleshooter for Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, told a Swiss newspaper his job would be to develop a plan for "preserving Switzerland's image abroad".

Diplomats said Cotti's decision to put Borer's task force in charge of the issue showed the government had recognised the seriousness of the allegations after an initial low-level response left the country appearing to be on the defensive.
"The government has now recognised the dimensions of the poblem and wants to create an adequate instrument for responding," said one Berne official, who declined to be named.

The Bankers Association said a senior diplomat like Borer would foster coordination among the government, commercial banks, the central bank and five separate commissions created or just being set up to look into Swiss financial dealings with Nazis and their victims before, during and after World War Two.
"This does not affect just the commercial banks, the government or the Swiss National Bank. It crosses the borders between them," spokeswoman Matile said.

Borer, 39, was named just two days after Cotti announced he was forming two expert panels to probe mounting accusations that the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims from Eastern Europe was used to compensate Swiss citizens for nationalised property.
In addition to the new panels on East Europe, Switzerland is tracking down accounts left by Jewish victims of the Holocaust and wealth stashed by Nazis in the neutral country in three ways.

A banking ombudsman is coordinating nearly 1,000 claims that have been submitted and an independent panel set up by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers will also comb banks' records for unclaimed wealth that may have escaped two previous sweeps.
Parliament is also set to give final approval in December to a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift strict banking secrecy and conduct a sweeping review of the era.
